::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) from farms deposits reactive nitrogen on downwind forests and thickens the canopy by up to $15\%$. Coupling GEOS-Chem to a dynamic vegetation model shows the extra leaf does two things at once: it pulls ozone out of the air through stomata (about $-2.1\text{ ppb}$ in $\text{NO}_x$-limited rural forest) and emits more isoprene that makes ozone where $\text{NO}_x$ is abundant (about $+1.4\text{ ppb}$ at urban fringes). After this module you can explain why the sign of the feedback is set by the local $\text{NO}_x$ regime, not by the nitrogen dose.
:::

## From farm ammonia to forest canopy

Three steps link a fertilised field to a forest canopy hundreds of kilometres downwind:

1. **Agricultural Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) Emissions**: Over-fertilized croplands and concentrated animal feeding operations volatilize millions of tonnes of reactive nitrogen gas.
2. **Atmospheric Transport & Wet/Dry Nitrogen Deposition**: Winds carry this reactive nitrogen downwind, depositing nitrate ($\text{NO}_3^-$) and ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$) onto natural temperate and tropical forests[^1].
3. **Vegetation Response**: Chronic nitrogen deposition acts as a nutrient amendment, altering plant biomass, canopy density (**Leaf Area Index, LAI**), and stomatal conductance.

### The dry deposition sink

Ground-level ozone is physically removed from the boundary layer through **stomatal uptake** and non-stomatal canopy surface destruction:

$$F_{\text{dry}} = -v_d [\text{O}_3] = -\frac{1}{R_a + R_b + R_c} [\text{O}_3]$$

where $R_c$ is canopy resistance. As nitrogen deposition increases tree leaf area ($\text{LAI}$), the total stomatal surface area increases, lowering canopy resistance $R_c$, accelerating dry deposition velocity $v_d$, and removing ozone from the air[^2].

### The biogenic VOC source

Plants synthesize **isoprene** ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$) and monoterpenes to protect photosystems from thermal and oxidative stress. Higher $\text{LAI}$ and nitrogen availability stimulate photosynthetic enzyme capacity ($V_{c,\text{max}}$), elevating biogenic VOC emissions:

$$\text{Isoprene} + \text{OH} + \text{NO}_x + h\nu \to \text{Peroxy Radicals} \to \text{Tropospheric }\text{O}_3$$

In urban and suburban perimeters with abundant anthropogenic $\text{NO}_x$ from cars and power plants ($\text{VOC}$-limited chemical regimes), additional biogenic isoprene fuels rapid photochemical ozone synthesis[^3].

## What the coupled model shows

In our study in *Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics*[^4], we simulated this feedback loop across East Asia under future agricultural emission pathways. The sign of the response follows the chemical regime, not the nitrogen dose:

| Region | Primary Chemical Regime | Dominant Mechanism | Net Surface $\text{O}_3$ Shift |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Northeast China (Remote Boreal Forests)** | $\text{NO}_x$-limited | Enhanced Stomatal Dry Deposition | **$-1.8\text{ to }-2.1\text{ ppb}$ (Cleaner Air)** |
| **North China Plain (Dense Agricultural Basin)** | Mixed transition | Dry deposition balances isoprene | **$-0.5\text{ to }+0.3\text{ ppb}$ (Neutral)** |
| **Yangtze River Delta (Industrial / Suburban)** | $\text{VOC}$-limited ($\text{NO}_x$-rich) | Biogenic Isoprene Photochemistry | **$+1.1\text{ to }+1.4\text{ ppb}$ (Smog Surge)** |
| **Southeast US (Oak-Pine Canopies)** | $\text{NO}_x$-limited rural | Dry deposition sink dominates | **$-1.2\text{ to }-1.6\text{ ppb}$ (Cleaner Air)** |

### Explore the regime dependence

Change the chemical regime and the deposition surge to see which term wins:

::: {.sim-card}
#### 🌲 Forest Nitrogen-Deposition Ozone Simulator

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ndep = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 40, step: 5, label: "Nitrogen deposition surge (%)"})
viewof regime = Inputs.select(new Map([
  ["Remote Rural (NOx-Limited)", "nox-lim"],
  ["Suburban Transition Zone", "trans"],
  ["Polluted Megacity Margin (VOC-Limited)", "voc-lim"]
]), {value: "nox-lim", label: "Atmospheric chemical regime"})

// The downstream gains are chained off the *rounded* LAI figure, as the
// original widget did, so the displayed numbers stay identical.
laiGain = Number((ndep * 0.16).toFixed(1))
vdGain = (laiGain * 0.9).toFixed(1)
vocGain = (laiGain * 1.12).toFixed(1)

o3 = {
  if (regime === "nox-lim") {
    const d = -(ndep * 0.021);
    return {text: d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#38bdf8",
      note: "🌿 NOx-Limited Remote Forest: Stomatal dry deposition dominates over biogenic VOCs, enhancing the natural vegetation ozone cleaning filter."};
  }
  if (regime === "trans") {
    const d = ndep * 0.003;
    return {text: (d >= 0 ? "+" : "") + d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#f59e0b",
      note: "⚖️ Transition Zone: Dry deposition sink and photochemical isoprene production nearly balance out, resulting in minimal net surface ozone shift."};
  }
  const d = ndep * 0.015;
  return {text: "+" + d.toFixed(2) + " ppb", colour: "#ef4444",
    note: "🏭 VOC-Limited Urban Fringe: Abundant anthropogenic NOx reacts aggressively with the surplus biogenic isoprene, intensifying summer smog episodes."};
}

card = (label, value, colour) => html`<div class="sim-readout">
  <div class="sim-readout-label">${label}</div>
  <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:${colour}">${value}</div>
</div>`

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${card("Forest LAI Expansion", "+" + laiGain.toFixed(1) + "%", "#10b981")}
  ${card(html`Deposition Velocity (<i>v</i><sub>d</sub>)`, "+" + vdGain + "%", "#38bdf8")}
  ${card("Isoprene Emission Flux", "+" + vocGain + "%", "#f59e0b")}
  ${card("Net Surface O₃ Response", o3.text, o3.colour)}
</div>`

html`<div style="font-size: 0.9em; background: rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.1); border-left: 4px solid #38bdf8; padding: 10px; border-radius: 4px;">${o3.note}</div>`
```
:::


### Data and code

- **Atmospheric Chemical Transport Model**: Simulations were conducted with the open-source **GEOS-Chem Model** (version 12.0.0).
- **Dynamic Vegetation Coupling**: Biophysical canopy responses were coupled using the **Community Land Model (CLM-DGVM)**.
- **Analysis Code**: Geospatial mapping and statistical scripts are available on GitHub: [`kamingfung/N-Deposition-Ozone-Feedbacks`](https://github.com/kamingfung).

## Key takeaways

- Agricultural ammonia is a forest fertiliser: downwind nitrogen deposition raises leaf area index by up to $15\%$.
- More leaf strengthens both an ozone sink (stomatal dry deposition, lower $R_c$) and an ozone source (isoprene emission); the local $\text{NO}_x$ regime decides which dominates.
- $\text{NO}_x$-limited rural forests get cleaner ($-1.8$ to $-2.1\text{ ppb}$), VOC-limited urban fringes get dirtier ($+1.1$ to $+1.4\text{ ppb}$), and mixed agricultural basins sit near zero.
- Air quality models that treat deposition velocities and biogenic emissions as static climatology miss this: agricultural policy feeds back into forest ozone sinks and sources.
- In suburban corridors around farmland, cutting industrial $\text{NO}_x$ is doubly useful, because it also stops the extra biogenic isoprene from becoming ozone.
